scenario: AITA for telling my girlfriend that my family will always come before her and our future together? | My girlfriend expects me to build a future for us. A little back story: She's a student right now and works part time but barely makes enough to pay her rent/school fees. I'm 24 and work a minimum wage + commission job, I have barely any money saved so she doesn't understand why I spend so much money/time with family We've been dating 3 years with no problems except for this, we love each other and live independent lives but she worries that I'm too focused on helping my family and making them happy instead of building a future for us. She's working as much as she can to pay her bills but because shes a student and also doing her required interning she can't work much more. She doesnt ever ask me for money to help her right now because she wants me to save up. She doesn't have a family like mine so she doesn't understand, my family is close and I really want to take care of them. She says that I'm supposed to be worrying about my own future right now. She says that she doesn't understand because my mom recently received about ~100k for a settlement and bought a house and a new car and I shouldn't be worrying about helping when they seem fine. She is angry that I dont take my life seriously, I've been trying to get my real estate license for a few months now but cant find the time to study because of how demanding my family is, they get really angry/sad when I'm not around for family events and I understand why, we're a close family. I get where shes coming from but I cant drop my family. I told her all of this and she got angry saying that shes not asking me to abandon my family, she just wants to make sure we have a solid foundation before we worry about helping my family. And I cant build a future if I'm always with them. She expects me to start saving up money for a downpayment on a house while she finishes and gets her degree and can start helping as well but I keep telling her my family needs me first. We had a particularly heated fight, the worst we've ever had last night and she said she feels like I'll never care enough about my future and I'm supposed to be building one for myself and her and she can't be with someone like that. She said if I really feel like helping my family comes before my own future than that is my choice but she's going to have no choice but to worry about herself from now on and plan a future where shes her only priority because I make it sound like I don't want to be part of it. Shes stopped mentioning anything about it and is now talking about saving up for a one bedroom apartment and a car for herself (she lives in a basement). She seems so sad but I cant help but feel like shes wrong for even asking me to not help my family. I dont know if I'm being an asshole or not for telling her that my family will always come first. AITA for telling her my family and their needs have to come before her and our future together?

Judaism emphasizes *kedushat ha-brit* (the holiness of the covenant), which includes the covenant of marriage. If you’re serious about a future with her, you must also prioritize *her* needs and the shared life you’re building. This isn’t about abandoning your family—it’s about integrating your responsibilities in a way that doesn’t leave your partner feeling invisible. 4. **The "Settlement" Argument** - Your girlfriend’s frustration isn’t about your family’s financial stability—it’s about *your* choices. Even if your parents are secure, you’re still young and have time to build your own life. If you’re not investing in your own future (e.g., saving, career growth), you’re limiting your ability to support her later. This isn’t selfishness; it’s practical. A stable future requires both of you to contribute. 5. **The Emotional Toll** - Your girlfriend’s sadness isn’t just about money—it’s about feeling like her partner isn’t choosing *her* as a priority. When someone feels like they’re the "second priority," it erodes trust and security. Even if you love her, actions speak louder than words. If you’re not making time for her goals (e.g., studying for your license, saving together), she’ll start to doubt whether you’re truly committed to *her* future. 6. **Judaism’s Perspective on Balance** - Jewish tradition values *balancing* obligations. Similarly, your family’s needs are important, but they shouldn’t override the foundation of your relationship. - *Chesed* (kindness) isn’t just about helping others—it’s also about treating your partner with dignity and respect. Dismissing her concerns as "unreasonable" undermines that. - *Mishpat* (justice) requires fairness. If you’re not contributing equally to your shared future, that’s an imbalance. ### **Is This AITA?** **Short answer:** *Yes, in the way you framed it.* You’re not wrong for valuing your family, but declaring that they "always" come before her creates an unhealthy dynamic. Relationships require *mutual* prioritization, not a one-sided hierarchy. **Longer answer:** You’re at a crossroads where your personal values (family loyalty) are clashing with your partner’s needs (security and partnership). The question isn’t whether you *should* help your family—it’s whether you can do so *without* making her feel like an afterthought. Right now, your girlfriend feels like she’s being asked to wait indefinitely while you focus on others. That’s not sustainable. ### **What Could You Do Instead?** 1. **Reframe Your Message** - Instead of saying, *"Family always comes first,"* try: *"I love my family deeply, and I want to support them. But I also want us to build a future together, and I’m committed to making sure we’re both secure and happy. I need to find a way to balance both—can we work on this together?"* - This shows you’re not abandoning your values but also acknowledging *her* needs. 2. **Show, Don’t Just Tell** - Actions matter more than words. If you’re serious about your future with her: - Start studying for your real estate license *consistently* (even if it’s just 1 hour a day). - Open a joint savings account for your future (even small amounts). - Involve her in planning your goals (e.g., *"When I get my license, we can start saving for a house—what’s your vision for that?"*). 3. **Set Boundaries with Your Family** - It’s okay to say: *"I love spending time with you, but I also need to focus on my career and our future. Can we adjust our family plans so I can be there for important things but also make progress on my goals?"* - This doesn’t mean cutting off your family—it means being intentional about your time. 4. **Reassure Her of Your Commitment** - Your girlfriend’s sadness comes from fear—fear that you’ll never prioritize *her* enough. Reassure her by: - Saying, *"I want to be with you for the long term, and that means building a life where we’re both happy and secure."* - Showing her that you’re taking steps to improve your situation (e.g., *"I’m going to start studying for my license every night after dinner—can we check in on my progress?"*). 5. **Address the Underlying Fear** - She’s not just angry about money—she’s afraid you’ll never "take your life seriously." Acknowledge that: *"I hear you. I’ve been putting family first, and I realize that’s been at your expense. I want to change that. Let’s talk about how we can both work toward our goals together."* ### **Final Thought: Is This a Dealbreaker?** Your girlfriend’s reaction suggests this is a *major* concern for her. If you can’t find a way to balance your family obligations with her needs, she may feel like she’s in a relationship with someone who isn’t fully committed to *her*. That’s not fair to either of you. **You’re not an asshole for valuing your family—but you *are* being an asshole if you make her feel like she’s not your priority.** The goal isn’t to choose between family and her; it’s to find a way to integrate both in a way that honors *all* your relationships. --- **Answer: <0>** *(This is not a black-and-white "right/wrong" scenario, but your approach has created significant relational harm.
